newsitem.title: USA: US Labor Dept unveils experimental CPI on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: US Labor Dept unveils experimental CPI on Thursday.

text.p: The Labor Department unveils an experimental Consumer Price Index on Thursday that should show cooler inflation but add more heat to the political debate surrounding the budget and Social Security.

Analysts expect the experimental system will only shave a few tenths from the CPI on an annual basis, far less than the 1.1 percentage point overstatement estimated by the Boskin Commission in a report to Congress last December.
The CPI, a measure of price changes from month to month, is used to set increases in benefits that millions of older citizens get through Social Security to make up for inflation.
It is also used to calculate tax brackets and personal income tax exemptions.
Budget savings from a more accurate cost-of-living measure could be enormous as Congress and the Clinton administration try to end the budget deficit by 2002.

But with voters' money at stake, both sides are reluctant to go first and take the political heat from setting a figure lower than the current CPI. For politicians the best solution would be a lower CPI produced by the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Tomorrow's experimental CPI report will use a geometric mean formula rather than a straight arithmetic approach. This was one of the recommendation's in the Boskin report.
For this reason it will be watched closely by those who think the current CPI must be fixed and those who argue that proof is lacking that the index overstates inflation.

The comparison of the two methods will cover recent years up until February. The Labor Department will issue the CPI for March, calculated under the existing method, next Tuesday. It rose 0.3 percent in February and 3.3 percent all of last year.

Many economists believe the experimental approach will more accurately reflect the so-called substitution factor in which consumers, faced with a price jump for one item, will seek to substitute it for something less expensive.

However, some question this, saying that so-called fixed weight systems for measuring price changes are inherently flawed and that some independent body will have to decide what the bias is and simply allow for it.
"In the end it will be a political call, not something that you can measure," said economist Michael Niemira of Bank of Toyko-Mitsubishi Ltd.

Defenders of those who live on the monthly Social Security check from the government say it is unconscionable to shave their annual inflation adjustment because of a technical change in a government index.

But Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, who first alerted lawmakers to the CPI overstatement, has argued that those living on modest fixed incomes can be helped in other ways rather than through an inaccurate index.
